item.text: [{"taxonId":47130,"summary":"A genus of flowering shrubs predominantly native to temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Members vary in their leaves, flowers and fruit: some have thorns, and their many-seeded berries include currants and gooseberries. Several species are cultivated for edible fruit, while the genus is also the main alternate host of white pine blister rust.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Several species have edible fruit, including blackcurrants, redcurrants, white currants and European gooseberries.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p2","s1:p13","s1:p18"]}},{"taxonId":47324,"summary":"A genus of annual flowering plants endemic to North America, where many of its roughly 20 species may be found in California. Its members are commonly called blue-eyed Marys or Chinese houses.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":47442,"summary":"A genus of perennial herbs, shrubs and, rarely, small trees native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas. Its cylindrical or rounded flower clusters have numerous long, slender stamens, creating a characteristic powder-puff appearance; flowering can continue year-round and is strongest in spring and summer.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":47450,"summary":"A genus of herbs and shrubs native to the Americas, eastern Africa, Madagascar, the Indian subcontinent and Indochina. Some members show rapid leaf movement; for example, Mimosa pudica folds its leaves when touched or heated. Their apparent globe-shaped flowers are actually clusters of many small flowers.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p7"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":47453,"summary":"A genus of trees and shrubs native to the Americas from Texas south to Peru. Members are cultivated for green manure, charcoal, livestock fodder and soil conservation; some species also have edible fruit or seeds.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Unripe fruits and seeds of L. leucocephala are edible; L. esculenta seeds are eaten with salt in Mexico.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p3"]}},{"taxonId":47555,"summary":"A genus of slow-growing, potentially very long-lived coniferous trees and shrubs occurring across temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere, with some populations in tropical highlands. Their single seeds sit partly inside bright red, berry-like arils. The sweet aril is edible, but its seed and every other part contain dangerous poisons and may be fatal if eaten.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"The sweet aril is edible only after its dangerously poisonous seed is removed; all other parts contain toxic taxine alkaloids.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p4","s1:p6","s1:p21"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p21","s1:p23"]}},{"taxonId":47603,"summary":"A genus of tap-rooted perennial herbs native to temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere. Its yellow-to-orange flower heads mature into round seed heads whose white, fluffy parachutes carry seeds on the wind; many species also form seeds without pollination. Leaves, stems, flowers and roots are edible, with greens eaten raw or cooked and roots roasted as a coffee substitute.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Leaves, stems, flowers and roots are edible; greens may be eaten raw or cooked, while roasted roots can substitute for coffee.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p7","s1:p8","s1:p31","s1:p33"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p31","s1:p32","s1:p33"]}},{"taxonId":47620,"summary":"A genus of flowerless vascular clubmosses; the supplied sources do not state a genus-wide native origin. Its usually creeping, forked stems are densely covered in small needle- or scale-like leaves, while upright tips bear cone-like spore structures.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":47696,"summary":"A genus of grasses native to Europe, the Azores, Algeria, Tunisia, Turkey, the Caucasus and Iran. Some members have been introduced to Australia and the Americas.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":47698,"summary":"A genus of flowering plants mostly native to Eurasia, with several species restricted to Greece and Turkey. Many have showy, fragrant purple or white flowers whose scent becomes more noticeable toward evening.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}}]
